newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ retail sector still in a trough - analysts.
newsitem.headline: NZ retail sector still in a trough - analysts.

text.p: New Zealand's retail sector is still in a trough despite encouraging data for April that showed a higher-than-expected rise in sales, analysts said on Tuesday.
Analysts said the monthly series was too volatile to draw firm conclusions from and that the sector was getting no assistance from the flat economy.

"We wouldn't be telling people that the time has come, the economy has turned. But it's further evidence that we are troughing along the bottom," said Warren Couillault, retail analyst at brokers SBC Warburg.
But the rise in April was at least a good sign for a sector that had endured six months of flat sales.
Statistics New Zealand said earlier that seasonally adjusted retail sales rose 7.9 percent in April, compared with a 3.9 percent fall in March and a 0.5 percent rise in April 1996.
Market expecations varied widely from a 2.0 percent fall to a 5.0 percent rise, the average being a 1.38 percent rise.
Commentators said the monthly series was notoriously volatile and difficult to draw firm conclusions from.
"You've got to look at the trend over the last two or three months," Bankers Trust NZ chief economist David Plank said.
Weakness in February and March was overstated, as was April's strength, Plank said.
More importantly, the three months to April had been flat, which was consistent with consumer confidence surveys, he said.
BTNZ does not expect any pickup until the year's end.

SBC Warburg's Couillault said anecdotal evidence suggested there was no definite trend up in sales. The last six months had been close to the bottom and the next six to 12 months were likely to completely bottom and then pick up, he said.
The exception were retailers who experienced "secular" growth quite outside the constraints of the economy.
In that category, companies like newly-listed fast food chain Restaurant Brands were picking up more than their share of retail spending.
"You also get companies that might be taking a lot of costs out at the moment that will have increasing leverage when the market picks up," Couillant said.
"Then you get companies such as The Warehouse, which just is steaming ahead in spite of no big increase in same-store sales or people flooding into the stores," he said.
"The reason they are still growing well, apart from their capacity expansion, is that they are filling up their stores with new product ranges," he said.

"The potential of The Warehouse is so untapped because you've got a huge franchise. If they can roll more categories through the stores then people will still go there but for wider range of product," he said.
Official data aside, home appliance retailer Pacific Retail said last that sales volumes had remained depressed, which had put the focus back on improved operating margins.
In March, clothing retailer Hallenstein Glasson painted a cautious picture for calendar 1997. In February, jewellery chain Michael Hill International said trading conditions had been difficult.

Supermarket chain Progressive Enterprises, which is in a restructuring phase, said in May that sales were down in its third quarter to April. Progressive is nevertheless expected to recover strongly in the current year due to re-positioning.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
